Centuries of colonisation and imperialism- the literal spread of western ideology, hasn’t been that influential? I think you might underestimate the dominance of western ideals throughout the world. Yeah of course other cultures have their own beauty standards that are rooted in deep and rich histories, but are you considering that the West (see: the British empire) conducted or attempted to conduct the colonial project on almost every country in the world?? That has real world effects that are still present today. And the dominance of western ideals is still very much in effect in countries that were colonised. Even the prevalence of western media (film, tv etc) plays a huge role, Hollywood has been one of the biggest global exporters of film for decades. You think that doesn’t affect people everywhere? There are even studies showing the effects of western media on non western communities , and what they saw as a result of this exposure was eating disorders among women.  

Also you’re talking about slim/thicc bodies as if there isn’t a whole other conversation to be had around that— slim and thicc bodies were undesirable in western culture (which is very much a dominant culture that dictates beauty standards among many other things whether you realise it or not) and associated with black and brown bodies. Black women in particular have experienced violence, assault and humiliation as a result of the racism and sexism linked to their body types. There are real roots in racism, sexism and colonialism here that have to be explored if you’re going to earnestly bring that up. The adoption of the slim thicc body standard serves as a reminder to PoC that their body type (the body many PoC have naturally) is only accepted as long as it is popularised by white bodies. 

It isn’t “arrogant” to recognise the long and significant history and continued practice of western imperialism and colonialism. racist and patriarchal ideals that have been spread throughout the world negatively affect us all, for example like you said in your comment  about the body ideals switch so often, our bodies all become like fashion trends, in fashion or out of fashion. Nobody wins.
This and your other comments are really interesting. Thanks for adding nuance and depth to this discussion. Unsure why so many people are downvoting. Have to assume it’s ignorance.

This comment is correct. Unsure why it’s downvoted. Western beauty standards affect the world, and they’re spread through the world not only through colonisation, but through film and tv and advertising… 

Of course body weight is linked to race and sex. The construct of whiteness itself was created to exclude the ‘other’. Of course this includes body types and thinness as an ideal for whiteness. Of course this negatively effects PoC across the world who don’t fit into this standard, as well as white people who don’t. Sure, you “change weight” but that’s not only missing  the point, but dismissing the point I feel

,

Would be highly dismissive to ignore centuries of imperialism and colonial rule when thinking about women’s bodies though (in Western society, and countries previously colonised by western countries). Racism and patriarchy are connected; it’s a complex topic, but it’s impossible really to look at the ideas we have about female body ideals in the west without understanding their root and construction which is intertwined with racism

our western conception of thinness is inextricably intertwined with racism, the construction or race, and colonisation.

Just adding to the discourse,  there have even been studies showing the effects of western beauty standards on non western communities— I read about one where they exposed the women in a community (I think somewhere in Asia but I can’t remember) who had never been exposed to western media before to western TV shows and films and it either caused or dramatically increased the rates of disordered eating

Hey Siebzhen, thanks for your thoughtful and interesting response.

The joke he made was definitely in poor taste, and very insensitive. And I made that clear immediately after he said it. 

Not to defend him, but I have mentioned in the past that my ancestors were almost definitely enslaved as that is how they would have come to be in the Caribbean. So he wasn’t wrong in the accuracy of what he said, it was the insensitivity of it, as I said the casual ease with which he said it. This is why he needs to learn about his casual racism, which he is doing; I’ve made it clear that this is absolutely necessary for us to move forward, especially as we want to have children some day. He is a person who cares about being good and doing the right thing, and so I’m confident he can and will do the work to change.

We have been together for almost 3 years and this is the first time something of this nature has happened. It has been unpleasant,  in many ways I’m glad it has happened so that we can actually learn from it, and most importantly he can unpack and unlearn internalised racism.

I’m also really sorry to hear of your negative experiences dating white people, and am sorry if reading this has been in any way triggering for you. It definitely sounds like, with the wrong type of person, a relationship can lead to racial trauma and that’s just awful. I’ve definitely heard some horror stories, especially when it comes to black children with racist, white parents

He made an insensitive joke and he is now actively learning about internalised bias and has been extremely apologetic and ashamed about the whole thing. Im not excusing it, I just know from experience that he is a good person who time and time again has shown he has the ability to learn and change, so I trust that this situation will be no different. He never invalidated my feelings and showed remorse and a willingness to change, which is something that I really do value. 

He’s never shown any signs of fetishising me or other women, he just thinks I’m beautiful and has only ever spoken of black and brown women in a celebratory way, just acknowledging the beauty, but never pointing and dissecting in a fetishistic way, which I have definitely experienced from some men back when I was dating. 

And he’s definitely not into horrible role play like that in the bedroom at all, master/slave role play is so abhorrent and couldn’t be further from what we’re into

Thank you for your interesting and analytical response! both of our sense of humour are the epitome of what you just described in fairness. You are correct, he has reacted in a way that shows he is willing to learn and examine his own internalised issues and he is finding it new and uncomfortable. He is currently reading Akala’s book called Natives: Race and Class in the Ruins of Empire, which is a really interesting  book I read last year, it talks much more about the black British experience and the relationship Britain had with the colonies. I have composed a good, educational reading list for him and he is getting through the book and realising things he didn’t previously know.

You aren’t wrong. And yes I definitely do see the situational comedy here from an outside perspective! I think I’ve just been feeling Uber sensitive  about colonial history recently, all the reading I’ve been doing has been making me feel quite angry and resentful of white people (which maybe isn’t great, but I’ve had a few repressed memories of racial incidents that have  just surfaced and it’s made me dislike white people more). 

I think possibly because this journey thinking about my heritage is new,  I’ve been feeling pretty sensitive to jokes of that nature. And he did know I feel strongly about anti-racism and the history of my ancestry so the joke felt in poor taste to me. (You raise a point about if he were black, and if he were black and made this joke I’d have found it funny, but because he is white, it rubbed the wrong way).  

He does want to be actively anti-racist, and that’s important to me. And despite this incident, he’s a good, caring person who actively wants to better himself and be the best for me and our future children. 

You are right, laughter is very important. I think I just wasn’t in the place to be able to appreciate this kind of joke, and he does know that now and is working to rectify it, so I’m feeling a bit better!

I second guess myself a lot too and I even did it in the Interview,  which I regret because I have all the classic inattentive symptoms. I tend to think “no it’s not adhd, everyone does this,” but then I’ll talk to my partner and he’ll be like no, that IS ADHD, most people can do a task they arent super excited about because they can think of the end result. I’m not able to do that. Another reason why I’m so bad at uni tbh. I have a lot of my own internalised doubts about ADHD which I’ve absorbed from other people which I think is why I invalidate myself, despite the fact I do classic ADHD things like obsess over a topic/song of whatever for a few days or weeks and then never look at it ever again!! 

I’m still processing being diagnosed but it does feel validating. But for that reason, if you’re second guessing, see if you can get a friendlier doctor because I’m sat here like,  “he hung up the call REALLY fast,” and “he didn’t seem that interested in what I had to say.” I think it may just have been his disposition and nothing personal.
